name: Fotogalleriet
overview: Non-profit kunsthalle for photography and camera-based art at Møllergata 34, 0179 Oslo (Store norske leksikon; Oslo Art Guide).

Opened on 5 September 1977 in a converted potato cellar at Oscars gate 50A, started by a group of photographers including Tom Sandberg, Dag Alveng, Bjørn Høyum, Per Berntsen, Jamie Parslow and Jim Bengston. The first show featured the British photographers Paul Hill and Raymond Moor (Store norske leksikon).

Store norske leksikon calls it the first exhibition venue in the Nordic countries to show only photographic and camera-based art. The foundation's own site calls it the longest-operating institution of its kind in the Nordic countries and the only kunsthalle in Norway focusing on art photography.
funding_verdict: Fotogalleriet: mainly public: Norwegian state culture funding, Oslo municipality and the Norwegian Photographic Fund

name: UKS (Unge Kunstneres Samfund / Young Artists' Society)
overview: Membership organisation for professional artists and an exhibition space for contemporary art at Keysers gate 1, Tullinløkka, in central Oslo (UKS website; Store norske leksikon).
Founded by artists for artists in 1921 (UKS website); its 2026 e-flux announcement says the founders were the Oslo avant-garde.
Membership of UKS includes membership of Norske Billedkunstnere (NBK); in 2024 it had about 700 members and was NBK's largest member organisation (Store norske leksikon).
funding_verdict: UKS: mainly public: the Norwegian Ministry of Culture, with an Oslo municipal grant

name: Vigeland Museum
overview: Museum in the former studio, home and planned museum of the sculptor Gustav Vigeland at Nobels gate 32 in Frogner, south of Vigeland Park (museum site).

In 1919 Oslo City Council decided to build him a studio. In a contract of February 1921 he left all his works to the city and kept the right to use the studio until his death. He moved in in 1924, died there in 1943, and the museum opened in 1947 (museum site).
Named for Vigeland.
funding_verdict: Vigeland Museum: public: the City of Oslo through its culture agency Kulturetaten

name: Perspektivet Museum
overview: The museum for the Tromsø area, with its exhibitions and offices at Storgata 95 in central Tromsø, a protected wooden merchant's house built in 1838 for the Mack trading family and used as Folkets Hus from 1911 to 2001 (Perspektivet, strategy 2023 to 2027).

The writer and painter Sara Fabricius, known as Cora Sandel, lived in a flat in the house as a young woman; the current exhibitions on the second and third floors start from her life and the house's history, with photography shown on the ground floor (Perspektivet).

The foundation was registered as established on 28 March 1995, to run museums and protect historic buildings in Tromsø, Balsfjord and Karlsøy (Brønnøysund Register); it took over the collections of Troms Folkemuseum and Tromsø Bymuseum and has been in the house since 2004 (Store norske leksikon).
funding_verdict: Perspektivet Museum: mainly public: Tromsø Municipality, Troms County and the Ministry of Culture

name: Tromsø Kunstforening (Tromsø Center for Contemporary Art)
overview: Members' association and free space for contemporary art, also named Romssa Dáiddasiida and, since its centenary, the Kven name Tromssan Taitopiiri; it calls itself the oldest art institution in northern Norway (tromsokunstforening.no; annual report 2025).
Founded in 1924; registered as an association with a founding date of 31 December 1924 (tromsokunstforening.no; Brønnøysund register).
Since 1981 its home has been Muségata 2 in Muséparken, a listed, municipally owned neoclassical building from 1894 built for Tromsø Museum (annual report 2025).
funding_verdict: Tromsø Kunstforening: mainly public: state, county and city operating grants, plus a rent-free city building

press_items.title: Hilde Sørstrøm and Carina E. Beddari, "Hakapik mener: Saken om Muségata 2 handler ikke bare om fasade" (2026)
Silvia Colombo, interview with Camilla Fagerli and Ruth Alexander Aitken (2025)

name: Munchs hus
overview: Museum in Edvard Munch's former house and garden at Edvard Munchs gate 25 in Åsgårdstrand, Horten municipality, on a slope with a view over the Oslofjord (museum site, Riksantikvaren decision).
Munch rented a house in Åsgårdstrand in 1889 and bought this one on a contract dated 25 August 1898 for NOK 900. The house is documented back to 1830 (Riksantikvaren decision).
Named for Munch, who died in 1944. Åsgårdstrand municipality bought the property from his heirs and the museum opened in 1947 (Riksantikvaren decision, Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Munchs hus: mainly public: state, Vestfold county and municipal money paid to the operator Vestfoldmuseene IKS

name: Vasl Artists' Association
overview: Non-profit artist-run organisation with a residency, a small gallery and an office at D-53/1, 1st Street, Block 4, Clifton, Karachi (Vasl).
Established in 2001 in Karachi. Adeela Suleman, now Executive Director, has been a volunteer since 2002 and is listed as a founding member.
Affiliated with the UK-based Triangle Network, founded in 1982 (Vasl).
funding_verdict: Vasl Artists' Association: privately funded: local patrons, art foundations and companies; no accounts published
wider_context: 7 September 2017: New York's Department of Financial Services fined Habib Bank and its New York branch 225 million dollars for failures to comply with New York anti-money-laundering and sanctions-screening rules. The release cites "Lack of evidence for adequate OFAC and sanctions screening" and says the bank handled billions of dollars of transactions with Al Rajhi Bank, which it describes as having "reported links to al Qaeda", without adequate controls. The bank agreed to surrender its New York branch licence (New York DFS). The order is dated history from 2017.
Vasl's pages name only "HBL" and "HBL Art Committee" as supporters, with no full name, and do not show that this is Habib Bank.

name: Dar Jacir for Art and Research
overview: Artist-run centre for art, research and agricultural exchange in the Jacir family home in Area A of Bethlehem, on the Hebron to Jerusalem road, near the separation wall and Rachel's Tomb (Wikipedia).
Founded in 2014 by Emily Jacir, with Annemarie Jacir and Yusuf Nasri Jacir listed as co-founders. Its full name is Dar Yusuf Nasri Jacir for Art and Research.
Named for Yusuf Nasri Jacir, whom Wikipedia lists as a co-founder.
funding_verdict: Dar Jacir for Art and Research: mixed private and grant-funded: crowdfunding, foundation and Swedish aid grants, a British Council fund
wider_context: Raid: Israeli soldiers raided the centre on 15 May 2021, damaged the building and took phones, computers, hard drives, cameras and books, according to the centre. Hyperallergic (Hakim Bishara, 18 May 2021) reported the account and that it was unclear if the centre was specifically targeted; no Israeli army statement appears in it or in The Art Newspaper (Hadani Ditmars, 19 May 2021).
Days earlier fires from Israeli projectiles destroyed the centre's Urban Farm (Hyperallergic).
Israel does not fund or control the centre, so this is state action against it, not state patronage of it.

name: The Freedom Theatre
overview: Theatre and youth arts centre in the Jenin refugee camp in the West Bank. It is registered as a nonprofit under the Palestinian Authority and as a foundation in Sweden, has a Palestinian team and an international advisory board (NPR).

Roots: the Stone Theatre, a community theatre started in the camp by Israeli peace activist Arna Mer Khamis in 1987 (NPR). Her son Juliano Mer Khamis, Zakaria Zubeidi and Jonatan Stanczak opened the Freedom Theatre in 2006 (Wikipedia).

An Israeli military operation destroyed the Stone Theatre in 2002 (NPR). Wikipedia states the original theatre sat on the top floor of a family house, destroyed by an Israeli bulldozer during the 2002 Battle of Jenin.
funding_verdict: The Freedom Theatre: foreign donor-funded: NGO and government donors named in its 2013 annual report, plus individual monthly donors

name: Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo
overview: Cultural centre of the Paraguayan National Congress in the former Cabildo (town council) building on Avenida de la República, between Río Manduvirá and Río Tebicuary, Asunción (Última Hora, 2021).

Opened on 14 May 2004 with Chilean president Ricardo Lagos and the writer Augusto Roa Bastos present; Carlos Mateo Balmelli, from the presidency of Congress, had the idea and carried it out with director general Margarita Morselli (ABC Color, 2019).
Morselli led it for 20 years until Aníbal Saucedo Rodas replaced her in July 2024 (La Nación).
funding_verdict: Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo: public: the Paraguayan National Congress's budget
wider_context: Última Hora says Congress holds seven other premises besides its main building, worth over G. 118,880 million by the Senate's own inventory, and recalls criticism of an officials' car park and a "quincho de oro" in its courtyard.
El Cabildo's extension is paid from the decree that article criticises.

Redacción ÚH, "Congreso tiene luz verde para gastar en construir un obelisco" (2025)

name: Pinto Art Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum at 1 Sierra Madre St., Grand Heights Rd, Antipolo, Rizal, outside Manila. It sits in the Silangan Gardens, a botanical garden of two hectares (pintoartmuseum.ph).
Founded in 2010 to show the collection of the neurologist and arts patron Dr. Joven Cuanang. Wikipedia says the Pinto Gallery opened in 2000 and became a museum in 2010.
"Pintô" means "door" in Filipino (pintoartmuseum.ph).
funding_verdict: Pinto Art Museum: privately owned: founder Joven Cuanang, with ticket and art sales

press_items.title: Katherine Alamares, "LA Exclusive: Pintô Art Museum's Former Curator Explains His Explosive Black Saturday Post" (2021), on Riel Jaramillo Hilario's Facebook post

name: Ayala Museum
overview: Private museum of Philippine history, art and culture at Makati Avenue corner De La Rosa Street, Greenbelt Park, Makati City.
Painter Fernando Zóbel envisioned it in the 1950s as a museum of Philippine history and iconography. It opened in April 1967 under the Filipinas Foundation, now the Ayala Foundation (Wikipedia).
Named for the Ayala group, the family business whose foundation runs it. Zóbel belonged to the Zóbel de Ayala family and worked for Ayala Corporation until 1961 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Ayala Museum: corporate-sponsored: run privately by the Ayala Foundation, with Ayala group co-presenters and partners

name: Green Papaya Art Projects
overview: Independent artist-run non-profit initiative in Metro Manila. The 17th Istanbul Biennial page describes it as the "longest-running independently run multidisciplinary initiative in the Philippines".
Founded in 2000 by artists Norberto "Peewee" Roldan and Donna Miranda. The group's own essay gives the founding date as 1 May 2000 (4A Papers).

It began in a condominium building near the University of the Philippines in Quezon City, then moved to a converted garage and a two-level apartment (Wikipedia). In August 2008 it moved into a two-storey building in Kamuning, Quezon City, and from around October 2015 the bar Catch272 occupied the ground floor (4A Papers).
funding_verdict: Green Papaya Art Projects: independent: small grants from cultural institutes, donations and shop sales

name: Jorge B. Vargas Museum and Filipiniana Research Center
overview: A museum of Philippine art and culture on Roxas Avenue in the University of the Philippines campus at Diliman, Quezon City, one of nine museums and galleries on the campus (Quezon City Government website).

Jorge B. Vargas (1890 to 1980) donated his collection to the University of the Philippines on 1 March 1978; the university laid the cornerstone in 1983, objects began moving to Diliman in 1986 and the building was formally inaugurated in 1987 (ASEF culture360).

What is there: oil paintings, watercolours, pastels, drawings and sculptures covering Philippine art from the 1880s to the 1960s, with works by Juan Luna, Felix Resurreccion Hidalgo, Fernando Amorsolo and Victorio Edades, all from the Vargas donation (ASEF culture360).
funding_verdict: Jorge B. Vargas Museum and Filipiniana Research Center: a state university museum; budget not published on the pages read
wider_context: Jorge B. Vargas served as Mayor of Manila in 1942 and as ambassador to Japan from 1943 to 1945 (ASEF culture360); the museum's holdings are his personal collection and papers.

name: Muzeum Sopotu
overview: Museum of the city of Sopot in a villa of 1904 at ul. Księcia Józefa Poniatowskiego 8, opposite beach entrance no. 29, with a garden holding a brine graduation tower (museum site).
Founded in 2001 by a decision of the Sopot City Council and the Mayor. The City Council adopted its current statute by resolution XXIV/395/2021 on 13 May 2021 (museum site, BIP).
Named for the city.
funding_verdict: Muzeum Sopotu: public: the City of Sopot's operating subsidy, with small own sales

name: Galeria Foksal (Foksal Gallery)
overview: Non-profit contemporary art gallery at ul. Foksal 1/4 in Warsaw, in an annexe to the Zamoyski Palace, named for the street it stands at the end of (stated by the gallery).

Founded in 1966 by the critics Wiesław Borowski, Anka Ptaszkowska and Mariusz Tchorek with artists including Tadeusz Kantor, Henryk Stażewski, Zbigniew Gostomski, Edward Krasiński and Roman Owidzki; Borowski was nominally its sole director for nearly 35 years (stated by the gallery). Gostomski's "Optical Objects" opened it on 1 April 1966 (English Wikipedia).
Gostomski, Krasiński and Zygmunt Targowski designed the interior, cabinets, bookshelves and chairs, which remain unchanged, and the lettering of its invitations and posters (stated by the gallery).
funding_verdict: Galeria Foksal: public: the Mazovia regional government, through the Mazovian Institute of Culture

name: Casa das Marinhas
overview: House at Rua 24 de Junho in Marinhas, Esposende, on a slight rise with a double-height living room facing the sea (municipal site).
Alfredo Evangelista Viana de Lima designed it and it was built from 1954 to 1957. The pages read do not say who commissioned it (municipal site, iconichouses.org).
Named for the Marinhas parish. The municipal page quotes Viana de Lima calling it "o solar dos tempos modernos", the manor house of modern times (my translation).
funding_verdict: Casa das Marinhas: public: the Município de Esposende

name: Hangar – Centro de Investigação Artística
overview: Artist-run centre for artistic research, exhibitions, residencies and studios at Rua Damasceno Monteiro 12 in the Graça neighbourhood of Lisbon (Hangar website, e-flux directory).

Mónica de Miranda says XEREM was founded in 2010. FIELD says Hangar was created in 2015, after XEREM's residencies and exchanges within the Triangle Network created a need for a permanent space (FIELD, Carlos Garrido Castellano, issue 6, winter 2017).
FIELD describes Mónica de Miranda as a founder and Bruno Leitão as Hangar's curatorial director and a board member.
funding_verdict: Hangar: small non-profit project: public and private grants, partnerships and studio rents

name: Beta-Local
overview: Artist-run platform for artistic practice in Puerto Rico and the Caribbean at Avenida Manuel Fernández Juncos 1412, San Juan. It describes itself as "an organization, a working group, and a physical space" (Beta-Local; e-flux directory).

Founded in 2009 in San Juan by the artists Beatriz Santiago Muñoz and José "Tony" Cruz and the curator Michy Marxuach, in response to the lack of local contemporary galleries, museums and art schools (e-flux, Marina Reyes Franco, 6 November 2018).
It has administered Casa del Sargento, a historic building in Old San Juan owned by the Puerto Rican Institute of Culture, since 2014 (e-flux directory).
funding_verdict: Beta-Local: foundation-funded: Mellon, Warhol and Rauschenberg foundations, and contributions

name: MARe / Muzeul de Artă Recentă
overview: A private art museum at 15 Primăverii Boulevard, Bucharest, in a building of 1,200 sqm on five floors (museum website) by the Lebanese architect Youssef Tohme (The Art Newspaper, 22 October 2018).

Roger Akoury founded it; the MARe Foundation, of which he is president, created and runs it, and it opened on 9 October 2018 with the art historian Erwin Kessler as director (museum website; The Art Newspaper, 22 October 2018).

The museum holds 1,000 artworks by more than 250 Romanian and international artists, among them Ion Țuculescu, Andrei Cădere, Horia Bernea, Ion Grigorescu, Dan Perjovschi, Hermann Nitsch, Lucio Fontana, Olafur Eliasson, Richard Long and Michelangelo Pistoletto; the international part covers 'the last six decades' (museum website). At opening it had around 550 works, assembled by Akoury with Kessler's advice (The Art Newspaper, 22 October 2018).
funding_verdict: MARe: private, one founder's money through the MARe Foundation, plus sponsors and tickets
